newsitem.title: UK: Russia, Turkey clash over shipping safety.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Turkey clash over shipping safety.

text.p: Turkey has clashed with Russia and other Black Sea nations over shipping safety in the narrow Bosphorus Strait, with traffic likely to increase sharply over the next few years, a senior Turkish maritime official said on Friday.

Mithat Rende, Turkey's delegate to the London-based International Maritime Organization (IMO), said measures promoted by Russia at an IMO meeting this week "would only serve the acceleration of traffic, not the enhancement of safety" in the Bosphorus.
Rende said some 50,000 vessels each year passed through the Bosphorus, which was only 700 metres wide at its narrowest point and ran through the city of Istanbul.
The Russian plan could "lead to calamity and disaster," he told Reuters.

Rende said Turkey had done much to improve safety in the last few years, and that the number of accidents in the strait had fallen sharply since it introduced new rules after a disaster in which several seamen were killed and 20,000 tonnes of oil were spilt in 1994.
"We are willing to respond to all constructive proposals," he said, adding that the talks had not reached a stalement. But Turkey was opposed to "political and economic point-scoring."
Rende stressed that the strait was entirely within Turkish territorial waters and no other country had a right to impose its will.
Navigation in the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles is unrestricted for commercial vessels under the 1936 Montreux Convention except in times of war.

The number of ships passing through the straits has soared over the last 60 years, and even more tankers could ply the waters once vast oil reserves in ex-Soviet Central Asia come onstream unless a costly new pipeline is built across Turkey.
Turkey wants the oil to be pumped from Baku in Azerbaijan to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan in order to reduce alleviate fears over safety in the Bosphorus.
